title: Why a Vision Needs a Feel for the Work
summary: Bennis said leaders do the right thing. Robert Sutton added a corollary: you can't pick the right thing without knowing what it takes to build it. How to stay close.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Kickoff meeting, slide twelve. The market is big, the story is clean and the whole roadmap fits on one slide as three colored bars. Then an engineer near the back asks how checkout will work, given that the payment partner's API allows a few requests a second and the plan assumes thousands. The answer comes with a smile: "That's an implementation detail. Let's not get into the weeds."

Nobody argues, and the meeting ends on time. But look at the team chat that afternoon. People pad their estimates, nobody volunteers the next risk, and the engineer who asked has learned that "how will this work?" isn't a welcome question here. The vision is still on the slide. Fewer people in the room believe it.

Doing things right, doing the right thing

Warren Bennis spent decades writing about leadership and left us one of the most quoted lines in management: "Managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing." Managers keep the current work running well. Leaders choose which work is worth doing at all. You may know the ladder version: climbing fast doesn't help if the ladder leans on the wrong wall.

It's a useful lens, and the previous post in this series, Over-Managed and Under-Led, leans on it. Even Robert Sutton, the Stanford professor who later pushed back on it, calls the distinction "more or less correct" and "useful to a degree" (True Leaders Are Also Managers, HBR, 2010). Trouble starts when people read it as a job description.

When a good line becomes an excuse

Sutton read through the leadership literature twice for his books, and this split kept bugging him. In that HBR post he describes what it does to some leaders: they "see their job as just coming up with big and vague ideas," and treat implementing them, or even talking through the details, as mere "management" work.

His examples will feel familiar. A cell phone company CEO never visited the stores that sold his phones, because that was beneath him, and kept pushing strategies built on a wrong picture of what customers went through. Project managers got IT and software projects with absurd deadlines, tiny staffs and small budgets, sometimes for things that weren't technically possible, and then took the blame when those projects failed.

In our world it's the roadmap with dates nobody estimated, or the "simple" migration that turns out to touch every service. Sutton's diagnosis fits both: "big picture only" leaders often decide without the constraints that drive cost and time, and keep pushing even as the evidence piles up that the plan can't be built.

Sutton's corollary

Sutton keeps the Bennis line and adds a corollary I'd tape to every tech lead's monitor: "To do the right thing, a leader needs to understand what it takes to do things right, and to make sure they actually get done."

Picking the right wall sounds like pure judgment, the kind you can do from far away. In practice you can't pick well without a feel for how heavy the ladder is, how far it reaches and how many people it takes to move it. A roadmap drawn without that feel is a wish list with dates on it.

Think of planning a dinner party when you've never really cooked. The five-course menu looks great on paper and everyone's excited. Then you're in the kitchen with one oven, two hands and a braise that needs two hours on its own, and you find out which parts of the plan were fantasy from the start. The menu is the what. The kitchen is the how. A menu written by someone who has never stood at the stove tends to promise an evening the kitchen can't deliver.

Zoom in, zoom out, repeat

The dreamers Sutton admires (he names Francis Ford Coppola, Steve Jobs, and Ed Catmull and Brad Bird at Pixar) think big and are still "willing to get very deep into the weeds." What he values is "this ability to go back and forth between the little details and the big picture." One example comes from Bill George, who told Sutton that in his first nine months as CEO of Medtronic he spent about 75% of his time watching surgeons implant Medtronic devices and talking with doctors, nurses, patients, families and hospital executives.

Rosabeth Moss Kanter at Harvard Business School calls the same skill zooming. In Zoom In, Zoom Out (HBR, 2011) she writes that the close-up and the wide view both have virtues and pathologies, and "should be vantage points, not fixed positions." Stay zoomed in and you chase quick fixes and one-off exceptions. Stay zoomed out and you can seem "remote and aloof," and miss the small signals that something is shifting. Her advice for the zoomed-out leader is practical: "broad visions need to be matched by small wins that demonstrate feasibility."

Nobody needs their VP reviewing variable names. What a team needs is a lead who knows when to drop into a detail, and who comes back up with a sharper picture.

Close to the work, hands off the keyboard

If you're thinking "this sounds like micromanagement," fair. The line runs between understanding the details and owning them. Owning them means taking the keyboard, dictating the how and leaving people no room to think. Understanding them means knowing enough to ask a sharp question, to sense when an estimate is fantasy, and to make a trade-off that survives the first week of real work.

You can hear the difference in one sentence. "Help me understand the trade-off here" keeps you close and leaves the work with the people doing it. "Just do it the way I said" takes the work and the thinking off their plate. Teams keep bringing problems to the first kind of lead. With the second kind, they slowly stop.

A few ways to stay close without hovering:

  • Read the design doc before the review meeting, and ask about the riskiest assumption in it.
  • Before you commit to a date, ask the person who'll build it what would make the estimate wrong.
  • Once a month, pick one on-call ticket or incident and read it end to end.
  • Join one real design discussion as a participant, and let someone closer to the code correct you.

Why it gets harder as you go up

The higher you go, the easier floating gets and the fewer people call it out. You can talk only in outcomes and themes, and "I'm at the strategy level now" sounds like a perfectly good reason not to know how the system works.

Kanter borrows a term from the economist Thorstein Veblen for what happens next: trained incapacity. Spend too long on work that uses only part of your repertoire, and the other part atrophies. A lead who hasn't read code or sat in a design debate for a year loses more than fresh context. Slowly, they lose the ability to tell a bold plan from an impossible one.

Sutton puts the stakes plainly. The worst senior executives, he writes, use the leadership-versus-management split "as an excuse to avoid the details they really have to master to see the big picture and select the right strategies." Doing the right thing and doing things right are two ends of one rope. Let go of one end and sooner or later you lose the right to pick the direction.

Try this week

  • Next time you hear "that's an implementation detail," ask what the detail is, and write the answer down.
  • Pick one roadmap item and ask the engineer closest to it what would make the date slip.
  • Read one design doc or incident report end to end, outside a meeting.
  • Catch yourself saying "just do it this way" once, and swap it for "help me understand the trade-off."

faqs.q: What did Warren Bennis mean by "managers do things right, leaders do the right thing"?
faqs.a: He was separating two jobs: running the current work well, and choosing which work is worth doing at all. Robert Sutton, who quotes the line in a 2010 HBR post, calls the split more or less correct and useful to a degree, but warns that some leaders use it to skip the details they need to understand.

faqs.q: What is Robert Sutton's corollary to the Bennis line?
faqs.a: "To do the right thing, a leader needs to understand what it takes to do things right, and to make sure they actually get done." In practice, you can't choose a good direction for a team without a rough sense of what it will cost to build.

faqs.q: Isn't getting into the details just micromanagement?
faqs.a: Understanding the details and owning them are different things. Micromanaging means taking the keyboard and dictating how the work gets done. Staying close means knowing enough to ask a sharp question, spot an unrealistic estimate and make a real trade-off, while the people doing the work keep deciding how.

faqs.q: What does zooming in and zooming out mean for a leader?
faqs.a: Rosabeth Moss Kanter used the image in a 2011 HBR article. Zooming in gives you sharp detail but can trap you in quick fixes; zooming out gives you context but can make you seem remote and miss early signals. She argues both should be vantage points you move between, and that broad visions need small wins that show they can work.

faqs.q: How can a senior engineering leader stay close to the work?
faqs.a: Read design docs before review meetings and ask about the riskiest assumption. Ask the person who will build something what would make the estimate wrong before you commit to a date. Read an incident report end to end now and then, and join a real design discussion as a participant.
